name: berbero di Sokna
catalog_citation: Sarnelli, Tommaso. 1924-25. Il dialetto berbero di Sokna: Materiali lessicali, testi manoscritti in caratteri arabi, con trascrizione e traduzione. Supplemento all'Africa Italiana. Napoli. (archive.org item sarnelli_1925_berbero_di_sokna, scanned djvu text)
catalog_locator: Introduction, section on transcription ('Trascrizione'), djvu text (printed page number not recoverable from scanned layer)
catalog_quote: Sulle vocali il segno + indica: lunga ed accentata ... lunga e atona ... breve e accentata ... brevissima e atona ... Ogni qualvolta capita di dover segnare l'accento e la quantità su di una vocale che già porti sovrapposto un altro segno fonetico, ciò vien fatto, per necessità tipografiche, nella maniera seguente ... Poichè il berbero di Sokna non si appoggia ad alcuna scrittura propria — quella in caratteri arabi essendo solo usata in via eccezionale — la trascrizione dei testi raccolti, come quella di tutti i dialetti berberi ed arabi nord-africani, mostrerà frequentissimi gli spostamenti dell'accento e della quantità, le oscillazioni ed alterazioni vocaliche e consonantiche. E' perciò che nei testi la rappresentazione fonetica di una stessa parola verrà a trovarsi variamente segnata, Per quanto riguarda la quantità, mi sono quindi attenuto, nel trascrivere le parole berbere, al solo…

(2) Deciding source: a 1924-25 46-page lexical-materials-plus-texts publication from one last-generation speaker; the deciding sentence is a transcription caveat, not an accent analysis. For Sokna it is nonetheless the best and essentially only primary source (Prasse 2019 EB 43 confirms; language extinct), so no instrumental/modern description competes. The three Encyclopédie berbère entries (Prasse 1998 El-Foqaha, Prasse 2019 Sokna langue, Souag 2019 Sokna sociolinguistique) and Souag 2020 (QSBLB 7), all downloaded and read, are silent on accent. sources.citation: van Putten, Marijn. 2014. A Grammar of Awjila Berber (Libya), based on Umberto Paradisi's material. (Berber Studies 41.) Köln: Köppe. [already. opened now, not re-downloaded]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'It has been suggested for other eastern Berber languages, such as Siwa and Nefusa and El-Foqaha, that a shift of accent approximately has the same function as État d'Annexion in other Berber languages (Brugnatelli 1986, Louali & Philippson 2005). In these eastern Berber languages, after prepositions and subjects in post-verbal position, the accent of the noun shifts to the penultimate position.'

sources.citation: Prasse, Karl-G. 2019. 'Sokna (Fezzan): langue' (S68). Encyclopédie berbère 43: 7476-7479. DOI 10.4000/14u37 (OpenEdition, open).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Phonology section covers absence of spirantisation, palatalisation of g/k, vowel system 'trois voyelles pleines a, i, u ... et une voyelle auxiliaire (?) ǝ, à place fixe'; no statement on accent/stress. States Sokna is known essentially only from Sarnelli's 1923 materials ('d'une qualité remarquable'), one consultant, 4-5 speakers in 1915, now extinct.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Sociolinguistic history only (Lyon 1821, Richardson 1850, Rohlfs 1881, Sarnelli 1924: 4-5 speakers; language shift completed soon after 1881); no phonology.

sources.citation: Prasse, K.-G. 1998. 'El-Foqahā' (F36). Encyclopédie berbère 19: 2886-2889. DOI 10.4000/encyclopedieberbere.1953 (OpenEdition, open).

sources.quote: Phonology section (spirantisation absent, palatalisation, 5-vowel system a i u ǝ ä, possible e) has no accent statement. Confirms Paradisi 1961/1963 are the only description of El-Foqaha, 'très sommaire, mais très sûre dans la notation'; about a dozen speakers in 1960.

sources.note: The one work that treats accent PLACEMENT in eastern Berber (Siwa, Nefusa, El-Foqaha; possibly Sokna) as a system - default position vs. penultimate shift after prepositions/post-verbal subjects (per van Putten 2014: 54). Our 'variable' coding rests on Sarnelli's remark that the same word is accented differently in texts vs. isolation, which is what such an alternation predicts; reading Brugnatelli decides whether the languoid has a statable rule.
